items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Asia Open
items.title: Kospi -6.5%: Samsung -8%, SK Hynix -9% as CXMT threatens the memory moat
items.idea: Kospi fell ~6.5% with Samsung off almost 8% and SK Hynix down 9%+. The new trigger is CXMT's plan to unveil a server-memory product on a new chip structure by year-end. Memory fundamentals are called solid, but the market is repricing the duration of the shortage-to-oversupply cycle.
items.angle: Memory is the purest leveraged expression of the AI buildout, and the first place a Chinese catch-up shows up in prices. Pairs with the US SOX six-day -12%.
items.tweetA: Kospi -6.5% is an index event, not a stock event: two names are the AI trade for an entire country. CXMT doesn't need to win, it only needs to make 'server DRAM stays scarce' an open question. That's all a crowded multiple needs to break. $005930 $000660 $MU
items.tweetB: Everyone priced memory as a toll road with one owner. A Chinese server-DRAM announcement turns it into a toll road with construction crews on the parallel lane. USD/KRW at 1,342 is telling you who's running for the exit.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Asia Open
items.title: Riyadh airport attacked, Ukraine energy 'ceasefire' already violated, and Brent is DOWN 1.2%
items.idea: Brent ~$105 and WTI ~$92.50 are lower despite an attack on Riyadh's international airport and fresh strikes on Ukrainian energy infrastructure right after Trump announced an energy agreement. Oil is treated as a correction, not a de-escalation signal.
items.angle: Crude futures are fading headlines while physical stress is elsewhere (see diesel cracks, tanker rates). Risk-premium complacency in the one market that matters for CPI.
items.tweetA: An airport in Riyadh gets hit, an energy ceasefire is broken within hours, and Brent trades down. Either the market sees through all of it, or paper crude is the last place the stress shows up. I know which one I'd bet on. $USO $XLE
items.tweetB: Trump declares a Ukraine energy deal. Russia strikes Ukrainian energy infrastructure anyway. Ceasefire half-life: shorter than a Brent daily candle.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Market Wrap
items.title: CoreWeave's 9.75% 2031 bond yields ~16%; Oracle 2033 prints record-low price
items.idea: CoreWeave's 2031 paper yields ~16%, its CDS has blown wider, Meta-related infrastructure paper sits near lows and Oracle's 2033 bond hit a record-low price. The framing: nobody doubts compute demand, the question is whether the capital structures financing it survive.
items.angle: Credit is now leading equity on AI. Wider spreads raise cost of capital, hit project economics, hit equity, hit confidence: a loop.
items.tweetA: A 9.75% coupon trading to a 16% yield means the bond is in the low 80s. Equity people are still arguing about TAM while the credit desk is pricing a haircut. When the two disagree, bonds have historically been right. $CRWV $ORCL
items.tweetB: The AI buildout is a financing story wearing a technology costume. Demand for compute isn't the question; whether the SPVs holding the GPUs can roll their debt at 16% is. Watch CDS, not the keynote.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Market Wrap
items.title: Hot CPI: hike odds hit >50% for Oct, Dec >95%, then Treasuries rallied as equities broke
items.idea: STIR priced October hike odds above 50% and December above 95% on the CPI print, but by afternoon some of it was pulled back as stocks and AI credit cracked. The market moved from trading an inflation problem to trading a financial-conditions problem in one session.
items.angle: Markets are doing part of the Fed's tightening. Sets up Warsh at the IMF as a test of which narrative wins.
items.tweetA: Hike odds went to 95% for December and bonds rallied anyway. The curve is saying the Fed won't need to finish the job because credit will. That's not a soft landing, that's tightening by accident. $TLT $SPX
items.tweetB: Warsh walks into Bangkok after a day where the market traded both sides of his policy argument. Inflation says stay tight; CoreWeave at 16% says be careful what you wish for.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Market Wrap
items.title: S&P through 7,775-7,750: dealer gamma goes from shock absorber to accelerant
items.idea: The S&P broke its first meaningful pressure zone around 7,775-7,750 where dealer positioning and gamma become less friendly. Hedge funds and long-onlys both sold across comm services, tech, discretionary, industrials. Positive gamma plus concentrated leadership had damped every wobble for months.
items.angle: A 53-day no-1%-down streak ending plus gamma flipping is a regime change in realized vol.
items.tweetA: For months every dip met a wall of dealer buying. Below 7,750 the same dealers stop absorbing and start amplifying. The streak ending at 53 days wasn't news; the gamma flip is. $SPY $VIX
items.tweetB: Six years without a 1% drop trained everyone to sell vol. One 1.1% day and the suspension is softer. How many portfolios are short convexity they don't know they're short?

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Market Wrap
items.title: Diesel cracks near $100 and dirty-tanker rates at multi-year extremes: the barrel is whispering, freight is shouting
items.idea: Following new attacks around Hormuz, diesel cracks near $100 and dirty-tanker freight at multi-year extremes show the supply chain carrying more stress than Brent reflects. If the gap closes via higher Brent rather than lower products, the inflation problem gets another leg.
items.angle: Product and freight dislocation is the leading indicator for the next CPI energy print and refiner earnings.
items.tweetA: Diesel crack at $100. Tanker rates at multi-year highs. Brent down on the day. One of these three prices is wrong, and it isn't the two that require a physical molecule to move. $VLO $MPC $FRO
items.tweetB: The inflation print came from energy and the stress is still migrating into products. If Brent has to catch up to diesel, September's 3.7% is a floor, not a ceiling.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom / Market Wrap
items.title: US government already takes equity stakes in semis and quantum: is AI credit stress the next candidate for a backstop?
items.idea: The US has taken direct equity stakes in strategically important companies, particularly semiconductors and quantum computing. If AI-related borrowers lose cheap private capital, the line between private financing and strategic state support thins. The market currently has no buyer of last resort.
items.angle: A state backstop would cap the downside in the credit loop but reprice equity as quasi-utility.
items.tweetA: If CoreWeave can't refinance at 16%, who's the buyer? Washington has already shown it will own pieces of chips and quantum. 'Too strategic to fail' is a trade, and nobody is pricing it. $CRWV $INTC
items.tweetB: AI-vs-China framed as national security means the Fed put gets a cousin: the CHIPS put. Private losses, public balance sheet, 2027 vintage.

items.angle: Gold is sitting on the multi-test support: a break would hit the whole metals complex.
items.tweetA: Silver -6% in a day, gold on the third test of $4,100 in a week. The $3,900-$4,100 floor was built over a year of lows. Supports don't get stronger each time you lean on them. $GLD $SLV
items.tweetB: Fed funds 3.75-4.00% and a coin-flip on a hike, with gold at $4,100. Real yields are the whole story for the next two weeks, not the war.

items.source: The Bubble Bubble / Precious Metals Update
items.title: Why gold sells off on an energy-driven CPI: supply-shock inflation is not debasement
items.idea: The author argues the Iran-war inflation (war now in month eight) is an energy supply shock, not monetary debasement, which is the type precious metals hedge. So a hot print raises rate expectations and hits non-yielding assets even though inflation itself is rising.
items.angle: Frames how to sort inflation regimes: monetary vs. supply. Different hedges.
items.tweetA: Gold doesn't hedge a supply shock, it hedges the policy response to one. When the response is hikes instead of printing, the 'inflation hedge' trades like a long-duration bond. Know which inflation you own. $GLD $TIP
items.tweetB: Eight months of war and CPI went 3.4 to 3.7. Gold's worst days have all been hawkish-repricing days. Debasement trade or real-rate trade? You can't be both.

items.title: Tax-loss selling begins in mid-October: TSX-V -3.55% to a 52-week low, lowest since Aug 2025
items.idea: Miners have been in a downtrend for nearly all of 2026 except six weeks in Jan/Feb and August; 2025's gains masked it. The TSX Venture Composite's 3.55% drop took it below its summer low, erasing the full mid-July-to-August rally round-trip, to the lowest since August 2025.
items.angle: Junior miners are the canary for retail risk appetite in metals. Early tax-loss selling = unusually many losers.
items.tweetA: Tax-loss selling in mid-October means the losers are so numerous people can't wait for December. TSX-V made a full round trip in two months. The 2025 gold story got people comfortable; 2026 miners kept telling a different one. $GDXJ
items.tweetB: Gold near $4,100 and the junior index at a 14-month low. Equities are discounting a lot less gold than the metal itself.

items.title: 'The semis are now in their 4th 10%+ correction since early June': most in this window since late 2002
items.idea: Bespoke: four 10%+ semis corrections since early June is the most inside a window that small since late 2002. Pairs with SOX -12% in six days.
items.angle: Repeated dip-buying success gets tested. 2002 was a different cycle regime (post-bubble).
items.tweetA: Four 10% corrections in five months and every one got bought. The last time this happened was 2002, and nobody wants to talk about what 2002 was. $SMH $SOXX
items.tweetB: Semis don't trend, they whipsaw: four 10% pullbacks since June is what a topping process looks like when the fundamentals haven't cracked yet. Or a rolling accumulation. Which one are you paid to know?

items.idea: Rubner: peak earnings blackout, 24% of S&P 500 index weight is outside repurchase blackout windows. Rises to ~55% at month-end, ~75% by Nov 3 (Midterm Election Day), ~85% by Nov 9.
items.angle: The largest marginal bid in the market is switched off during the selloff. The window reopens right into the midterms.

items.idea: The streak of consecutive days without a >=1% drop ended at 53, the longest since 2020. A Daily Chartbook dashboard studies forward returns after streaks of 50-59 days.
items.angle: Low-vol regime break; check the forward-return study before assuming mean reversion.
items.tweetA: 53 days without a 1% drop, then 1.1%. Vol streaks don't end quietly: they end on a day when the cause is a hot CPI and a credit bond at 16%. $VIX $SPX
items.tweetB: Short-vol is the most crowded 'free lunch' in the market. 53 days is the longest since 2020. You know how 2020 ended.

items.title: CPI diffusion is DOWN even as headline CPI rose to 3.7%: Warsh's preferred lens
items.idea: Anna Wong's tweet: diffusion of CPI inflation, measured like Warsh's preferred PCE diffusion metric, is falling. That conflicts with the 'broad inflation' read of the print used by the hawks.
items.angle: Gives Warsh a dovish talking point on Thursday: breadth is narrowing, energy is the story.
items.tweetA: Headline CPI 3.7% and the breadth of price increases is falling. If Warsh's own diffusion metric says energy, not broad inflation, the hike odds are priced on the wrong chart. $TLT
items.tweetB: Two readings of one CPI print: Dark Side says broad, the diffusion index says narrow. The Fed chair picks the lens. Ask who he's been reading.

items.title: Forward revenue/earnings revisions breadth rose through the bull market; ICYMI: '1998-2000 internet bubble analog climax'
items.idea: Yardeni: share of S&P 500 companies with positive 3- and 12-month forward revenue and earnings revisions rose significantly during this bull. ICYMI headlines teased: 'We have now reached the climax of the 1998-2000 internet bubble analog', 'VIX upside convexity has gone extremely bid while SPX downside convexity remains very offered', 'Investors are aggressively betting on a sudden turnaround in interest rates' (headlines only).
items.angle: Fundamentals (revisions) are strong while positioning signals scream topping.
items.tweetA: Revisions breadth is rising while the vol surface prices a crash. Fundamentals and options don't usually disagree this loudly for long. One of them is mispriced. $SPX
items.tweetB: The 1998-2000 analog is back in my feed twice this week. In the analog, Oct 1999 was a correction before the final 40%. Not saying. Just noting where we are on the map.

items.title: Anthropic told investors it made $16.8B in Q3 revenue and turned profitable on an adjusted basis (Bloomberg)
items.idea: Quarterly revenue (not run-rate) of $16.8B with adjusted profitability, relayed on a day the Nasdaq fell ~1.9% and the S&P ~1.1% on inflation and AI-financing fears.
items.angle: Counter to the AI-credit narrative: a frontier lab is cash-generative while neoclouds borrow at 16%. Value is migrating from infra owners to model owners.
items.tweetA: $16.8B in a quarter and profitable. A year ago people argued whether the labs could cover inference costs. Now CoreWeave yields 16% while its biggest customer category prints profit. The risk isn't demand, it's who holds the balance-sheet risk. $CRWV $AMZN $GOOGL
items.tweetB: $16.8B a quarter is $67B annualized and still not the number that matters. What matters is how much of it flows to the GPU landlord vs. stays with the model company.

items.title: OCP/SEMICON/DigitalOcean field notes: agents are a CPU+memory+storage story, 800V power, optics demos, fab and DC labor pools overlap
items.idea: Agents execute code, access tools and retain state, so CPU, memory, storage and scheduling enter the economics beside inference (Part 2 of a CPU series coming). Wiwynn/Ayar Labs/GUC and Credo optical demos carried traffic; Delta's 800V hardware made the power transition tangible. A SiTime rep linked agentic workloads to demand for higher-performance timing. Applied Materials says cleanroom availability and skilled construction trades are constraints, with fabs and data centers drawing on overlapping labor pools.
items.angle: Diligence leads: CPUs for agents, timing (SiTime), 800V power, skilled trades as binding constraint.
items.tweetA: Everyone's pricing GPUs. Agents also need a CPU for every tool call, state in memory, and a scheduler. The bill of materials for 'keeping an agent working' is a different shopping list than training. $INTC $AMD $SITM
items.tweetB: The binding constraint on fabs and data centers might be electricians, not wafers. Both are pulling from the same labor pool. Wage inflation in skilled trades is a second-order AI capex cost no model includes.

items.title: Contrarian: Anthropic's $16.8B Q3 is well under pace for the $100B+ ARR exit target; year-end ARR maybe $85-90B
items.idea: After the $16.8B Q3 revenue headline, P Equity argues the more concerning detail is that Anthropic is tracking below its previously targeted $100B+ ARR exit; ARR may end around $85-90B.
items.angle: Same data point, opposite read vs BEP. Useful for the 'AI monetization' debate.
items.tweetA: Two newsletters, same $16.8B: one calls it proof, the other says it's tracking to miss a $100B exit-ARR target by $10-15B. A 'miss' that is still 10x+ year-over-year growth is the strangest bear case in markets.
items.tweetB: Missing a $100B ARR target by landing at $85-90B. If that's a disappointment, the market has priced in growth that has no precedent in enterprise software. Priced for perfection at a size nobody has reached.

items.title: Starshield limits: Musk says US government owns/controls it, speed and usage set by US military 'and ultimately POTUS'
items.idea: Ukraine reported unannounced restrictions (reportedly cutting military-grade connectivity above 100 mph) that hit drones and air defense during a Russian assault; Zelensky said 'people will die'. Musk said Starshield is government-owned and limits are decided by the US military. No public evidence ties it to a presidential order or the refinery-strike dispute. The piece's point: the owner, not the operator, holds the leverage; a network restriction can simply appear.
items.angle: Defense-tech dependency risk: allied militaries will want sovereign constellations (Europe: IRIS², etc.). Space/defense positioning.
items.tweetA: Ukraine's drone war runs on a network where the 'speed limit' can be changed by someone who isn't Ukrainian. Every European MoD just read that. Sovereign LEO comms goes from nice-to-have to procurement line. $RKLB $ASTS $AIR.PA
items.tweetB: A weapons restriction can be debated in parliament. A bandwidth restriction just appears. That is a new kind of leverage in alliance politics, and it's software-defined.

items.title: Things happen: Netflix to lay off ~1,000, biggest cuts since 2022; YouTube Music launches AI-generated music labels
items.idea: Netflix plans to cut 1,000 employees, its steepest since 2022 (BBC). YouTube Music introduced labels identifying songs generated entirely or partly by AI, including AI in composition or vocals (TechCrunch).
items.angle: Media/content: cost reduction at the market leader plus provenance labeling as the response to AI floods.
items.tweetA: Netflix cutting 1,000 while content spend stays enormous. Streaming's margin story is now an employee-count story. And YouTube Music labeling AI songs is the first sign that provenance, not generation, is the scarce asset. $NFLX $GOOGL
items.tweetB: Labels on AI music are the 'organic' sticker of the 2020s. First mover in provenance becomes the toll booth for authenticity.

items.title: Small private-equity managers are struggling most to sell aging assets (PEI Group fund-performance report)
items.idea: PEI Group's latest quarterly fund-performance report shows small PE managers have the hardest time exiting aging assets; headline asks if the worst is over or yet to come.
items.angle: Fits the alt-manager stock drawdown: the public marks are ahead of private marks.
items.tweetA: Small PE funds can't sell old assets. Their LPs can't get distributions. Their LPs then can't commit to new funds. The denominator effect has a 2026 edition. $APO $KKR $BX
items.tweetB: Public alt managers are down 45% from their highs because the listed market is the only mark that moves. Private marks lag by 3-6 quarters. That's the gap.

items.title: DOJ gives California 48 hours to investigate potentially ineligible voters and set aside unverifiable mail ballots, threatening emergency court action
items.idea: Three weeks before the midterms, DOJ set a 48-hour deadline for California on noncitizen voting checks and unverifiable ballots, threatening emergency court action (Axios).
items.angle: Election-administration conflict risk into Nov 3 combined with the buyback window reopening that day.
items.tweetA: A 48-hour DOJ ultimatum to the largest state's election office, three weeks before the midterms. Whatever your politics, the market-relevant fact is the tail: contested results mean a longer vol window. $VIX
items.tweetB: Midterm Election Day is also when about 75% of S&P buyback capacity reopens. Mechanical bid meets political uncertainty.

items.title: Private equity's public pain: all six listed alt managers down 3%+ intraday; basket 45.3% below high, as deep as COVID
items.idea: APO, ARES, BX, CG, KKR, OWL are all down >20% YTD. OWL -5.5% on the day (down >2/3 from Jan 2025 peak), KKR best at -1.8%. KKR and CG are roughly half off highs; APO 36.5% below peak. The equal-weight basket quadrupled at its early-2025 peak and is up 115% this decade but sits 45.3% below its high, deeper than the 2022 bear market.
items.angle: Alts are the credit canary for the AI-debt financing story (private credit funds finance data centers).
items.tweetA: The alt-manager basket is deeper in drawdown than 2022 and about even with COVID, with no recession. Every rebound has topped lower. Equity markets are pricing something credit markets haven't printed yet. $OWL $KKR $APO
items.tweetB: Private credit funds are the lenders for the AI buildout. Their stocks are down 45%. That is the market telling you the collateral is worth less than the marks.

items.title: Energy sector closes +50% YTD for the first time in 2026: only the third year since 1990, all since 2021
items.idea: Energy's YTD gain passed 50%; since 1990 only three years had it (2021, 2022, 2026). The record fastest was May 17, 2022; this took more than twice as long but still ranks fifth among qualifying sector-years. Tech accounts for 7 of 16 instances. Consumer Discretionary, Staples, Industrials, Materials and Real Estate have never been up 50%+ in any year.
items.angle: Energy as the leader of an inflationary-war bull; XLE concentration is a positioning flag.
items.tweetA: Sector up 50%+ YTD has happened 16 times since 1990. Tech 7, Energy 3. Three of those 16 were energy, and all three came in the same five years. Commodity supply shock is the regime. $XLE $XOP
items.tweetB: Energy +50% while the S&P is breaking support and CPI is 3.7%. This is what a stagflation-lite tape rewards: own the thing causing the inflation.

items.title: Bull market turns four: S&P +118.26% (4th-best first four years vs. 9-bull avg 97.5%), but the typical stock lags
items.idea: Monday marked four years since the Oct 2022 low. Only the 9th bull to run 4+ years. Gains of 118.26% trail only bulls from April 1942, August 1982 and March 2009. Under the hood, the typical stock's performance is less remarkable (premium section cut off).
items.angle: Index-vs-median-stock divergence is the structural story behind the concentration risk now unwinding.
items.tweetA: S&P +118% in four years, 4th best ever. Median stock: not even close. We've had a four-year index bull and a two-year average-stock stagnation. The semis correction is where that distinction gets settled. $RSP $SPY
items.tweetB: Only three bulls did better in their first four years: 1942, 1982, 2009. Each was followed by more upside. Each also started from a depressed base; this one started from rates at zero. Different launch pad.

items.title: 'Time to stop renting your AI': Reflection AI CEO says enterprises move to own models; open-source went from ignored to default in six months
items.idea: Misha Laskin compares AI to real estate: renting works at first; once you spend hundreds of millions on models, owning makes sense, giving control of data and costs. 'Six months ago no one was talking about open source and now it's the opposite.' Reflection trained a US open-source competitor (Beam) to Chinese labs with a small team in about a year.
items.angle: Open-weight models raise a question for token-revenue businesses; enterprise buy-vs-rent inflection.
items.tweetA: Frontier labs are growing on rented intelligence. Enterprises spending hundreds of millions a year start doing the buy-vs-lease math. At some scale every CFO does it. That's the tail risk for token revenue. $MSFT $NVDA
items.tweetB: Rent vs own: a US open-source lab with a small team caught up in a year. If the moat is 12 months of lead time and weights are open, the value is in the compute and the data, not the model.

items.title: Hackers heated French supermarket fridges, causing fires and food losses (Reuters); Cursor launches its first in-house model, Composer
items.idea: Relevant-links section: Reuters reports hackers manipulated refrigeration at French supermarkets, heating the fridges, sparking fires and food losses. Also Simon Willison on Cursor launching Composer, its first in-house model.
items.angle: Cyber-physical attacks on retail cold chain: insurers and OT security. Cursor shifts from model customer to model builder.
items.tweetA: Hackers cooked the fridges in French supermarkets. Fires and spoilage, not ransomware. Cyber risk just crossed from data loss to physical loss, and cyber insurance wasn't priced for that. $CRWD $PANW
items.tweetB: Cursor ships its own model. The application layer is vertically integrating into the model layer. Everyone who rents tokens from a lab is a future competitor of that lab.

items.title: Meta's first frontier model, Muse Wonder / Wonder Full: 'Active Memory' and 'Active Focus', claims parity with Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra
items.idea: Released Monday, aimed at 'personal and professional agentic tasks'. Active Memory carries context across conversations; Active Focus keeps working toward the goal and recovers from errors. Meta's internal numbers: roughly on par with Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra and ahead of them (and Opus) on MemoryBench. Reactions mixed; T3 Code users like it as reviewer / part-time orchestrator.
items.angle: Memory as differentiator; Meta's capex now has a flagship to show. Still self-reported benchmarks.
items.tweetA: Meta says Muse Wonder beats Opus on MemoryBench. Self-reported, and on a benchmark Meta's team presumably tuned for. But the real news: Meta's frontier model lands the same week their AI capex bonds trade near lows. $META
items.tweetB: Persistent memory is the next battleground: whoever holds your context holds your switching costs. Meta has the social graph and now a memory model. That's the combo to watch.

items.title: OpenAI names its third head of compute in under two years; compute spend plan up to ~$750B through 2030 from ~$600B
items.idea: Uday Ruddarraju replaces Sachin Katti (who locked in a 10GW lease with SB Energy backed by an Nvidia guarantee). The Stargate lead left for Meta earlier this year; another build leader left in August. Parekh: every GW is $50B+; OpenAI's plan is ~30GW by 2030, and it lacks the free cash flow of Google or Meta.
items.angle: Execution risk at the largest buyer of compute: a leading indicator for neocloud and Oracle backlogs.
items.tweetA: Third compute head in two years, at a company that has to build 30GW. At $50B per GW that's $1.5 trillion of plans managed by a rotating cast. Revolving-door leadership on the biggest capex program in history is not on any risk slide. $ORCL $NVDA
items.tweetB: OpenAI's compute budget grew $150B in nine months while its infrastructure lead changed twice. The ceiling isn't chips or power. It's the number of people alive who've run a $50B build.

items.title: CoreWeave: $35B raised YTD, ~$52B debt and leases, ~$25B cash burn expected; courting insurers' 'unlimited' capital as 2032 bonds yield 14.8% and shares fall 15%
items.idea: CFO-side figures: over $35B raised across chip-backed loans, HY bonds, converts and equity this year; ~$52B of debt and lease obligations; analysts see ~$25B burn. The goal is investment-grade ratings so insurers can fund it. Bonds ~14.8%, stock -15% in a day. CoreWeave says 2027 capacity is nearly sold out; critics flag long data-center leases against shorter customer contracts.
items.angle: Maturity mismatch: long leases vs. shorter contracts is the textbook neocloud risk.
items.tweetA: The plan is to get an investment-grade rating so insurers can fund it, on a day the bond yields 14.8%. Insurers buy assets to match 20-year liabilities, not 3-year GPU contracts. Do the duration math. $CRWV
items.tweetB: Sold out through 2027 and the bond yields 15%. Either the market doesn't believe the backlog, or doesn't believe the renewals in 2028. The second is the real question.

items.title: ASML: orders being discussed for 2029-30, Q3 profit EUR4.96B vs EUR4.1B exp., FY sales EUR44-45B; planned +30% capacity in 2027 and 2028 won't be enough
items.idea: Net profit crushed expectations; ASML will upgrade installed tools, sell faster new versions and raise prices from 2027. Fewer than 100 EUV machines a year at $400M+ each. TSMC's prudence on capex pacing shapes ASML's book.
items.angle: Pricing power + backlog out to 2030 is the offset to memory worries. Semicap is the picks-and-shovels with order visibility.
items.tweetA: Customers are already placing 2029-30 orders for a machine that costs $400M. When the equipment supplier raises prices and still can't fill the book, capex isn't slowing; supply is the limiter. $ASML $AMAT
items.tweetB: Korea memory down 9%, ASML guiding orders through 2030. The equipment maker and the chip maker are seeing different cycles. One of them is wrong about 2029.

items.title: GTA VI (Nov 19): 40M expected copies, >$3B in 4 months; Rockstar headcount 2,441 to 4,711 since 2018; trailer 300M+ views
items.idea: Per Bloomberg: analysts expect 40M console copies and >$3B in four months; GTA V sold 230M and GTA Online still earns ~$0.5B a year. Eight-plus years, two delays, dev cost likely >2x the $500M publishers try to stay under; PC version early 2027; online version 2027.
items.angle: Take-Two as an event-driven catalyst; consumer-discretionary supply of attention in Q4.
items.tweetA: A single entertainment product with an expected $3B in four months is bigger than most film franchises' lifetime. Rockstar doubled headcount to build it. In an AI-budget world, the most valuable media asset is still hand-built. $TTWO
items.tweetB: GTA V: 230M copies, still ~$500M/year a decade later. That's an annuity with a hit-game's pricing. Take-Two's valuation question is how many years GTA VI Online earns like that.

items.title: 'Voluntold' AI adoption: unlike the bottom-up PC wave, AI is pushed down the org by top management
items.idea: AI-RTZ #1239 case study of publishing's AI revolt: adoption is being mandated from the top, the reverse of the PC wave where workers organically found uses for word processors and spreadsheets.
items.angle: Adoption-curve quality: mandated usage can inflate seat counts without producing productivity.
items.tweetA: The PC spread because workers wanted it. AI is spreading because executives want it. Mandated adoption shows up in license counts first and in productivity data last, if ever. $MSFT $CRM
items.tweetB: When the CEO says 'use the AI', the employee hears 'train your replacement'. Publishing is the early case where that turned into open revolt.

items.source: AI Snake Oil (Gabriel Unger & Arvind Narayanan)
items.title: There's a quiet gold rush to capture 'process traces' of human work (Mercor, Meta studying its own employees)
items.idea: Coding agents work because GitHub holds every step of software development; no such public traces exist for law, medicine, science. Companies like Mercor and Meta are capturing process traces from workers to train agents. The authors argue the same data could build 'white box' agents that expose intermediate steps instead of just replacing workers.
items.angle: Training data for non-coding professions is the next scarce input, with labor-market implications.
items.tweetA: Coding agents got good because GitHub is a free archive of how engineers think. Law, medicine and finance don't have one. The next AI data moat is employee screen recordings. Who owns your keystrokes? $META
items.tweetB: Imagine coding agents trained only on compiled binaries instead of source. That's every other profession right now. The first industry to publish its process traces gets automated first.

items.source: AI Snake Oil (Gabriel Unger & Arvind Narayanan)
items.title: Policy tilts toward automation: US tax treatment favors capital over labor; the agent 'trilemma': autonomous, reliable, general (pick two)
items.idea: The authors say US tax policy favors automation, labor got two-thirds of income for much of the 20th century, and the 'automate and compensate' UBI bargain is outside US political economy. They also frame a trilemma: fully autonomous, reliable in high-stakes settings, truly general-purpose: pick two. Proposals: research prizes, procurement, competition policy against lock-in, worker voice in AI deployment bargaining.
items.angle: Regulatory path for AI labor policy; a policy lever markets haven't priced (tax treatment of capex vs payroll).
items.tweetA: The tax code subsidizes the machine and taxes the worker. Add AI capex expensing and you get a firm-level incentive to automate before the tech is reliable. Policy isn't neutral on the automation question; it already picked a side. $SPY
items.tweetB: Autonomous, reliable, general: pick two. Every AI-agent vendor deck shows all three. The first earnings call that admits the tradeoff reprices a sector.

items.title: 'Pause, pivot, or accelerate: SaaS in the age of agentic AI': insurance leaders from Guidewire, Bessemer, SAP debate modernization
items.idea: Email is a promo for a McKinsey Insurance practice piece: agentic AI is reshaping the case for modernization in insurance, with leaders from Guidewire, Bessemer Venture Partners and SAP on how insurers should respond given existing commitments. Body content is teaser-only; analysis lives in the linked article.
items.angle: Incumbent core-system SaaS (policy admin) vs agentic rebuilds: a test of 'SaaS is dead' in a regulated vertical.
items.tweetA: Insurers are being asked whether to pause, pivot or accelerate core-system modernization because agents change what a policy admin system has to do. Vertical SaaS with long contracts is the first place the 'SaaS is dead' thesis gets a real test. $GWRE
items.tweetB: Guidewire, SAP and a VC in the same panel is the whole debate in miniature: incumbent, platform, and capital. Whoever's wrong has a multi-year contract to unwind.
